# --- Summary (read these first) ---
Part 1 summary: how the story starts
column2: At Christmas in Camelot, King Arthur's famously courteous Round Table court is feasting when a giant, entirely green knight rides into the hall on New Year's Day and dares anyone to strike him with his axe and take the same blow back in one year and one day.

column1: Part 1 summary: the beheading and Gawain's promise
column2: When the court hesitates and Arthur grabs the axe himself, Sir Gawain takes the game in his uncle's place and beheads the Green Knight, who picks up his own head and orders Gawain to the Green Chapel next New Year, so Gawain's life and honor now hang on his word.

column1: Part 1 summary: Gawain sets out and finds a castle
column2: After All Saints' Day Gawain rides alone through a brutal winter, reaches a magnificent castle on Christmas Eve whose lord (Bertilak) says the Green Chapel is nearby, and agrees to trade each day's winnings with him, which sets up the hidden test of Part 2.

column1: # --- Big takeaways ---
The opening frame from Troy to Arthur
column2: The poem opens with translatio imperii, tracing power from fallen Troy through Aeneas, Romulus, and Felix Brutus, who founds Britain, so Arthur's story is framed as the latest wonder in a land where more strangeness has happened than anywhere else.

column1: The Green Knight's challenge at Camelot
column2: At Arthur's New Year feast a huge green knight carrying a holly sprig and an enormous axe offers a Christmas game in which he takes one stroke now and gives the return stroke in one year and one day, testing whether the Round Table deserves its reputation.

column1: Gawain takes Arthur's place in the game
column2: Gawain, Arthur's nephew, claims the game so the king will not risk himself, beheads the Green Knight with one stroke, and is left bound by his sworn promise to receive the return blow at the Green Chapel next New Year.

column1: Gawain's arming and the pentangle shield
column2: Before leaving Camelot Gawain is armed and given a scarlet shield painted with a gold pentangle, the endless knot of fidelity that suits him because he is "fully faithful in five ways five times over," with Mary's image inside so his courage would not crack.

column1: Gawain's lonely winter journey
column2: Gawain rides alone through north Wales and the Wirral asking everyone about a Green Chapel, fights serpents, wolves, wodwos, bulls, bears, boars, and giants, and suffers even more from sleet and cold until Christmas Eve.

column1: The two promises Gawain makes at Bertilak's castle
column2: At Bertilak's castle Gawain swears to obey his host's will ("You may trust my tongue") and agrees to a bargain in which whatever the lord wins hunting in the woods is traded each evening for whatever Gawain gains at the castle.

column1: # --- Events in story order ---
How the Green Knight appears at Camelot
column2: At Camelot's New Year feast, just as the starters are served and Arthur is still waiting for a marvel before he will eat, a huge but handsome knight who is entirely emerald green, on a green horse, appears in the doorway and leaves the court speechless.

column1: Why the Green Knight says he comes in peace
column2: At Camelot the Green Knight wears no armor and points to his holly stem as proof he means "no menace," saying he is "clothed for peace, not kitted out for conflict" and only wants a game.

column1: How the Green Knight mocks the Round Table
column2: When no knight at Camelot answers his challenge, the Green Knight scoffs that the Round Table's towering reputation has been "skittled and scuppered" by a stranger and laughs until Arthur, red with anger, seizes the axe himself.

column1: How Gawain asks Arthur for the game
column2: Seated beside Guinevere, Gawain asks his uncle Arthur to step aside, calling himself the weakest knight whose loss would be "least lamented" and saying such a foolish affair is unfitting for a king, and the whole court agrees.

column1: The terms Gawain repeats before striking
column2: Before the blow at Camelot, the Green Knight makes Gawain state his name and swear to seek him out himself for the return blow, but refuses to say where he lives until after he has been struck.

column1: What happens after the beheading at Camelot
column2: Gawain's stroke cuts clean through the Green Knight's neck so the head rolls across the floor, yet the Green Knight does not stagger, picks up his head by the hair, and swings back into the saddle.

column1: The Green Knight's parting charge to Gawain
column2: Holding up his severed head at Camelot, the Green Knight tells Gawain to keep his word and come to the Green Chapel as New Year dawns, where men know him as the Green Chapel knight, or "be called a coward forever."

column1: How Arthur treats the marvel
column2: Though awestruck, Arthur tells Guinevere not to be daunted because such strangeness suits Christmas, has Gawain hang up the axe behind the dais as evidence of the event, and finally eats.

column1: The turning of the year before Gawain rides
column2: Fitt II opens with the year passing through Lent, spring, summer, and autumn until winter returns, and as Gawain prepares to leave the Camelot court hides its sadness by making jokes.

column1: Gawain's reply to the worried Camelot knights
column2: When the knights of Camelot grieve that Gawain must take a blow without striking back, Gawain calmly answers them that whether fate is kind or cruel, a man must still try.

column1: Why Camelot thinks Gawain's quest is a mistake
column2: As Gawain rides away, the court whispers that it would have been wiser to make him a duke than let him be beheaded by an ogre through "headstrong pride," and questions the king's judgment over a Christmas game.

column1: How Gawain finds the castle on Christmas Eve
column2: Lost in a frozen forest on Christmas Eve, Gawain prays to Mary for a house where he can hear mass, crosses himself three times, and immediately sees a castle so perfect it looks cut from paper.

column1: How the castle lord welcomes Gawain
column2: The castle's red-bearded lord (later named Bertilak) tells Gawain to do whatever he pleases in his house, and when the household learns its guest is the famous Gawain they expect to learn perfect manners and "love's tender language" from him.

column1: The two ladies Gawain meets in the castle chapel
column2: At evensong in the castle chapel Gawain meets the lord's young wife, lovelier than Guinevere in his eyes, hand in hand with an ugly ancient lady (later revealed as Morgan le Faye), and he bows low to the old one and courteously kisses the young one.

column1: Gawain and Lady Bertilak during the Christmas feasting
column2: Through the Christmas feasting at the castle Gawain and Lady Bertilak sit together enjoying whispered, refined conversation "free from foulness," which foreshadows the bedroom tests of Part 2.

column1: Why Gawain tells Bertilak he must leave
column2: When Bertilak asks what drove him from Camelot in midwinter, Gawain explains to him that he must find the Green Chapel and its green guardian by New Year's Day and would "rather drop dead than default from duty."

column1: How Bertilak keeps Gawain at the castle
column2: Bertilak laughs and tells Gawain the Green Chapel is nearby and a guide will take him there on New Year's morning, so Gawain can rest in bed while Bertilak hunts and Lady Bertilak keeps Gawain company.

column1: # --- Themes ---
Romance versus epic heroism
column2: Where Beowulf gave the epitome of the Germanic hero, Gawain is the ultimate romance hero in the chivalric sense, tested in manners, wit, and fidelity as much as in arms.

column1: What Gawain's adventure really tests
column2: Gawain's adventure tests not only his own knighthood but Arthur's court and, in a larger sense, the worth of chivalry itself.

column1: Where civilization's source seems to lie
column2: The plot suggests that the source of civilization lies in the heroism not of strong arms but of good manners, wit, and elegance.

column1: How trouthe will be tested unexpectedly
column2: Gawain sets out eager to prove his fidelity at the Green Chapel, but his troth will be tested in ways he does not expect, so by the time he faces what he thinks is the real test, that test is already partly over.

column1: Effictio portraits in Fitts I–II
column2: The poem uses long effictio for the Green Knight's green appearance, for Gawain in his armor, and for Lady Bertilak together with Morgan le Faye.
